where-the-representative-is-at-every-mom.text: The custody state diagram starts with no representative. Minting the Insert action token creates a pending Insert that holds no NFT. A Withdraw returns it to nothing. A fold on an absent key mints the representative into application custody, where application updates move it between successor UTxOs. The application releases it into a pending Update or Delete, which holds the only NFT there is, and only a valid fold burns it.
A pending Insert holds no NFT; a pending Update or Delete holds the only one. Nothing but a valid fold moves a representative out of a terminal request.

mint-move-and-burn.text: The table gives, for each transaction, what happens to the request token and to the representative: Insert creation mints an action token and no NFT; folding Insert mints the representative; an application update moves it; creating Update or Delete moves it into the request; folding them burns it; Withdraw mints a Withdraw action token and nothing else.

insert-certify-first-check-absence-when-.text: The sequence diagram runs from the user's proposal, through the application policy approving it and minting an Insert action token whose name hashes the proposal, to a pending request with no NFT, then to any folder proving absence, the registry recomputing the action name, minting the representative into the certified output and consuming the request. The key moves from absent to Active.
Certification approves the proposed creation, not a claim the key will stay absent. Two pending Inserts can target the same key; the one that sees absence at folding succeeds.

withdrawing-a-pending-insert.text: The sequence diagram shows the user asking to cancel one exact pending Insert, the application policy minting a Withdraw action token whose name commits to that UTxO and the refund terms, and Singular's spending witness checking the policy, recomputing the name and consuming the request with nothing minted and the registry unchanged.
Original Insert approval alone cannot cancel. Refund economics and disposal remain open.

application-evolution-keep-the-same-repr.text: The sequence diagram shows the application spending script consuming its UTxO and creating a successor carrying the same NFT and a new state, with no registry request, mint or burn. The key stays Active.

update-and-delete-transfer-authority-int.text: The sequence diagram shows the application spending script authorizing one exact release, moving the existing representative into the request, the request holding it with no withdrawal or sweep possible, a folder proving the existing value, and the registry consuming the request and burning the representative: Update sets Over, Delete sets absent.
Merely being able to spend the NFT does not authorize every operation. Terminal requests are completion-only.

what-batching-establishes.text: A fold applies operations to successive map states; absence and old-value checks belong to the native mechanics. One representative cannot sit in two pending terminal requests, and a consumed request cannot be consumed again. Replay across Delete and reinsert is not settled here.

where-the-lifecycle-is-going.text: The custody story above is unchanged by the settled interface: the representative is still minted on insert, still moves between successor application outputs without a registry request, and is still burned by the fold that ends the key. Three things are added around it.

A read is a request like insert or delete: it proves that a key holds a value against the root the fold has reached at that request's position, it changes nothing, and for a terminal key it entitles the requester to a terminal token. Reads ride folds with writes or alone.

An absent token witnesses a known absent key. It is created by inserting the absent state, lives in the cage's own custody so any later fold can consume it without a signature, and is consumed by the booking that ends the absence or by a delete. Terminal tokens witness a terminated key: any number, each minted by a folded read, each true forever, each freely burnable. The naming application's Over witness is one of these.

The sequence diagram shows a requester submitting a read of terminal with a tip, a folder including it in a batch, the registry verifying it against the root reached at its position and requiring one terminal token to the requester's output, with the leaf unchanged and the batch atomic.

Update keeps its meaning, the move to the terminal state, and delete keeps its meaning, the key is unknown again and may be booked afresh as the same key. What the interface removes is the pinned consumer script that today re-walks every batch; that binding becomes the cage's own check, generalised to all three token kinds.
